title: Automating resident billing without losing human control
metaDescription: Resident billing software in nursing homes (EHPAD): what can be automated, where to keep human approval and how to avoid errors before invoices go to families.
contentHtml:
Useful resident billing software in a nursing home (EHPAD) pre-calculates invoices and flags anomalies, but it leaves final approval to your administrative team. The billing clerk no longer enters every line: they check a short list of doubtful cases before sending. This split is what lets you automate resident billing without losing control over what families receive.

A resident's invoice combines rules that come from several places: the facility's accommodation rate, the dependency rate tied to the GIR, aid from the département (the French county-level authority: APA, social accommodation assistance), the residence contract and additional services. Every month, these rules have to be applied to data that changes: absences, hospitalizations, GIR changes, new notices. This article details what lends itself to automation, what must stay human and how to run the project safely.

Key points
  • A resident's invoice rests on two main rates, accommodation and dependency; care is funded by the French national health insurance (Assurance Maladie) and is not billed to the resident.
  • According to service-public.fr, the APA in a facility helps pay the dependency rate, but the share corresponding to the rate for GIR 5 and 6 remains payable by the resident.
  • Pre-calculation can be automated; approval, social assistance cases and replies to families stay human.
  • Anomalies must arrive sorted by financial impact, with the source that explains them.
  • Run the tool alongside your current method for several cycles before any switchover.

What makes up a resident's invoice in a nursing home?

A resident's monthly invoice mainly adds up an accommodation rate and a dependency rate, plus any additional services. The care component is funded by the Assurance Maladie as a lump sum paid to the facility: it does not appear as a line for the resident to pay.

The accommodation rate

The accommodation rate covers housing, meals, upkeep and activities. It is usually the largest line on the invoice. For a resident who receives social accommodation assistance (ASH, aide sociale à l'hébergement), the département covers part of these costs, and the resident contributes from their own resources according to rules set by the département, as detailed in the service-public.fr page on social accommodation assistance.

The dependency rate and the dependency lump sum

The dependency rate covers help with activities of daily living. It varies according to the resident's GIR (groupe iso-ressources, autonomy group), from 1 for the most dependent to 6 for the most autonomous, assessed with the AGGIR grid. The APA (allocation personnalisée d'autonomie, personalized autonomy allowance) in a facility funds part of this rate for residents classified in GIR 1 to 4. According to the service-public.fr page on the APA in a facility, a contribution equal to the dependency rate for GIR 5 and 6 remains payable by the resident.

In practice, the dependency lump sum requires the billing department to know three things every month: the GIR in effect, how the APA is paid (to the resident or directly to the facility, depending on the département) and the effective date of each change.

Additional services and special cases

The residence contract may include options: laundry for personal clothing, hairdressing, guest meals, telephone, outings. On top of these come adjustments: absences for hospitalization, admission or departure mid-month, death. Each follows a rule from the residence contract or from the département's social assistance regulations, and this is often where errors creep in.

Why is resident billing in nursing homes so prone to errors?

Nursing home billing is exposed because it combines stable rules (set rates, contracts) with data that changes during the month (attendance, GIR, notices), entered in different tools. The error rarely comes from a wrong calculation: it comes from information that was not carried over in time.

The data needed is scattered. Attendance and hospitalizations are in the care software. Additional services are in a schedule or a notebook. APA and ASH notices come from the departmental council, often by mail. The options taken are in the residence contract. The billing clerk links all of this together, from memory or by rereading.

The rules also vary from one resident to another. Two residents in the same room can have very different invoices depending on their GIR, their social assistance status and their options. For a group with several facilities, the département rules change again from one site to the next.

Finally, the error is visible. A family that finds a line billed during a hospitalization, or an APA adjustment with no explanation, loses trust far beyond the amount at stake. The administrative department then spends time explaining, correcting and reissuing.

Which billing errors come up most often in nursing homes?

Resident billing errors fall into five groups: absences not carried over, GIR changes not taken into account, aid applied incorrectly, additional services forgotten or billed twice, and admission or departure adjustments prorated incorrectly. They all have one thing in common: a data source that was not cross-checked with the invoice.

AnomalySource to cross-checkWhat the team checks
Absence for hospitalization not deductedCare software (movements)The absence rule in the residence contract or the département regulations
GIR change not carried overAGGIR assessment, care recordThe effective date and the dependency rate applied
APA or ASH applied incorrectlyNotice from the departmental councilThe amount, the period covered, the payment method
Additional service forgotten or doubledSchedule, service slips, contractThe option taken and the service actually provided
Admission, departure or death prorated incorrectlyAdministrative fileThe dates and the applicable billing rule

GIR changes deserve special attention. A change alters the dependency rate, the share still owed by the resident and sometimes the APA amount. If it is entered in the care record without being passed on to billing, the gap can last several months and lead to an adjustment that is hard to explain.

The trap: correcting the invoice without correcting the source data. If the absence is not entered in the care software, the error will come back the following month, whether the invoice is made by hand or by a tool.

What can be automated in resident billing?

You can automate everything that consists of gathering data and applying a written rule: pre-calculating invoices, cross-checking sources and detecting gaps. You do not delegate what requires judgment: an ambiguous social assistance case, a goodwill gesture, a reply to a family.

Pre-calculating invoices

Pre-calculation starts from the rules in effect (set rates, each resident's residence contract) and the month's data. It produces a proposed invoice for each resident, line by line, with the origin of each amount. The billing clerk no longer starts from a blank page or from last month's invoice copied over.

Matching the sources

This is the core of the automation. The tool reconciles the care software for attendance and movements, the schedule for additional services, the département's notices for the APA and the ASH, and the individual contract for options. When two sources contradict each other, it does not decide: it flags.

Detecting and sorting anomalies

Anomalies are ranked by financial impact: first the gaps that change the amount significantly (aid not applied, long hospitalization not deducted), then minor inconsistencies. The team handles a short list of qualified cases instead of rereading every invoice of the month line by line.

This is the difference between a tool that executes fixed rules and a tool able to read a situation. Classic automation stops as soon as the data is not in the expected format; the article on the limits of classic robotic automation in healthcare explains why.

How do you keep human approval over invoices?

The safest method is to make approval mandatory before any sending: no invoice goes out unless a team member has approved it, individually or as part of a batch. The billing clerk becomes a reviewer rather than a data entry clerk, and their sign-off remains the last step.

Decide what is approved as a batch and what is approved one by one

Invoices with no anomaly, identical to the previous month apart from changes in attendance, can be approved as a batch after spot checks. Flagged invoices are reviewed one by one. Sensitive situations always stay in individual review: a resident's first invoice, a death, a change in social assistance status, a dispute in progress.

Require a justification for each amount

Each proposed line must show where it comes from: the rule applied, the data used, the date. An approver who cannot trace back to the source is signing blind. This traceability also helps in case of an audit or a complaint; the article on what an agent must log in healthcare details what to keep.

Stay in control of the rules

Billing rules (rates, absence rules, options) must be readable and editable by the administrative management, not buried in technical settings. When the département publishes a new rate order, the team updates the rule and checks it on a few test invoices.

The right habit: record in the tool the reason for each manual correction. After a few months, these notes show which rules deserve a review or which entries arrive too late.

What must resident billing software do to stay under your control?

Resident billing software stays under your control if it shows its reasoning, if it cannot send on its own and if it flags instead of silently correcting. These are three questions to ask any vendor or provider before signing.

  • Readability: each proposed amount points to its rule and its source data.
  • Blocked sending: no invoice is issued without a recorded approval, with the approver's name and the date.
  • Flagging rather than correcting: when two sources contradict each other, the tool raises an alert and does not choose for you.
  • History: successive versions of an invoice are kept, with the reason for each change.
  • Connection to existing tools: the tool reads your care software and your current billing software, without forcing you to change them.
  • Health data: attendance and GIR are health data; their hosting must comply with the applicable framework, presented in the article on the regulatory framework for AI in healthcare.

For a management team running several facilities, add one criterion: a consolidated view of anomalies across all sites, with each one's specific département rules. The article on managing multi-site groups covers this organization.

When cross-checking sources takes several days each month, that is precisely the part worth handing off. With Granit agents, data collection and the sorted anomaly list are ready before your review; your team keeps approval and sending.

How do you roll out automation safely?

The project runs in four steps, and the most important is the third: run the tool alongside your current method before trusting it with production. As long as the two results do not match, you do not switch over.

  1. Audit the existing rules. List the rates in effect, the absence rules, the residence contract options and the département rules specific to each site, including those that are written down nowhere.
  2. Configure the rules and connect the sources. Translate each rule into the tool and link it to the care software, the schedule and the département's notices.
  3. Run in parallel over several cycles. Produce invoices both ways for several months and analyze each gap: tool error, manual error or misunderstood rule.
  4. Switch over with approval kept in place. The tool produces, the team approves. Human approval is not a transition phase: it stays in place.

Auditing the rules is often the most revealing part. It brings unwritten practices to light: a discount granted to a long-standing resident, an absence rule applied differently depending on the billing clerk. These cases must be settled by management before being configured, otherwise the tool will reproduce the inconsistency.

Choose the switchover month carefully. Avoid a month with a rate change or a large wave of APA notice renewals: you want to test the tool on a normal cycle before facing a busy one.

How do you know whether automation delivers on its promises?

You measure it with a few indicators tracked every month, before and after the switchover: the time spent on billing, the number of invoices corrected after sending, the number of complaints from families and the time between the end of the month and the issuing of invoices. Without a measured starting point, no improvement can be claimed.

The number of reissued invoices is the most telling indicator. An invoice corrected after sending means an error the review did not catch. It should go down; if it does not, look first at the source data, then at the configured rules.

The issue date matters too. Invoices sent on a fixed date, with a clear breakdown, reduce questions from families and speed up collection. An invoice that arrives late or is poorly explained delays payment and opens the door to disputes; the article on collections without dehumanizing the relationship covers what comes next when an unpaid invoice appears.

To go further on choosing indicators, the article on back-office KPIs in healthcare offers a framework that administrative management can use. What matters is to measure the same things before and after, on the same group of residents.
